exam.model: Suppose some assignment makes the formula false. A conditional is false only when its hypothesis is true and conclusion false, so \( (P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to R) \) is T and \( P \to R \) is F. From \( P \to R \) false: \( P = \) T and \( R = \) F. From \( P \to Q \) true and \( P = \) T: \( Q = \) T. From \( Q \to R \) true and \( Q = \) T: \( R = \) T. This contradicts \( R = \) F. So no assignment makes the formula false, and it is a tautology.
exam.prompt: Prove that \( \big( (P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to R) \big) \to (P \to R) \) is a tautology. You may either give a complete truth table or argue by assuming the formula is false under some assignment and deriving a contradiction.
rubric: If using the contradiction method: formula false requires hypothesis T and P → R F
P → R false forces P = T, R = F
Then P → Q true forces Q = T, and Q → R true forces R = T, contradicting R = F
Concludes no falsifying assignment exists, so it is a tautology (or a correct 8-row table with final column all T)
exam.why: This is hypothetical syllogism, the rule that lets you chain implications.

eg  ig( (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P)  ig) && 	ext{biconditional} \ &\equiv 
eg (P 	o Q) \vee 
eg (Q 	o P) && 	ext{De Morgan} \ &\equiv (P \wedge 
eg Q) \vee (Q \wedge 
eg P) && 	ext{negated conditional, twice} \ &\equiv (P \wedge 
eg Q) \vee (
eg P \wedge Q) && 	ext{commutative.} \end{aligned} \]
Here "negated conditional" is \( 
eg (A 	o B) \equiv A \wedge

Using the laws of logic (naming each), prove that \( 
eg (P \leftrightarrow Q) \equiv (P \wedge 
eg Q) \vee (
eg P \wedge Q) \).
rubric: Rewrites P ↔ Q as (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P)
Applies De Morgan to get ¬(P → Q) ∨ ¬(Q → P)
Uses ¬(A → B) ≡ A ∧ ¬B on each disjunct
Arrives at (P ∧ ¬Q) ∨ (Q ∧ ¬P), commuting as needed
exam.why: The negation of "same truth value" is "exactly one is true".

exam.model:
\( \neg \exists M > 0\ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ \lvert f(x) \rvert \le M \equiv \forall M > 0\ \exists x \in \mathbb{R}\ \lvert f(x) \rvert > M \).

For \( f(x) = x \): let \( M > 0 \) be arbitrary. Take \( x = M + 1 \). Then \( \lvert f(x) \rvert = M + 1 > M \). Since \( M \) was arbitrary, the negation holds, so \( f \) is not bounded.
exam.prompt: A function \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) is **bounded** if \( \exists M > 0\ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ \ \lvert f(x) \rvert \le M \). Write the negation with the negation pushed all the way in, and use it to prove that \( f(x) = x \) is not bounded.
rubric: Negation: ∀M > 0 ∃x ∈ ℝ |f(x)| > M
Restrictions M > 0 and x ∈ ℝ unchanged; ≤ becomes >
Proof takes an arbitrary M > 0 and exhibits x depending on M, e.g. x = M + 1
Checks |x| = M + 1 > M
exam.why: The negation's structure dictates the proof: "for every \( M \)" means start with an arbitrary \( M \); "there exists \( x \)" means construct \( x \), which may depend on \( M \).

exam.model:
If-then form: "For every real \( x \), if \( x^{2} > 4 \), then \( x > 2 \)."

Statement: false. At \( x = -3 \), \( x^{2} = 9 > 4 \) but \( x > 2 \) fails.

Converse: "If \( x > 2 \), then \( x^{2} > 4 \)." True: if \( x > 2 \), then multiplying \( x > 2 \) by the positive number \( x \) gives \( x^{2} > 2x > 4 \).

Contrapositive: "If \( x \le 2 \), then \( x^{2} \le 4 \)." False, with the same counterexample \( x = -3 \): \( -3 \le 2 \) but \( 9 > 4 \). This agrees with the fact that a conditional and its contrapositive always share a truth value.
exam.prompt: With domain \( \mathbb{R} \), consider "\( x^{2} > 4 \) only if \( x > 2 \)." Write it in if-then form, and give the truth value (as a statement about all real \( x \)) of the statement, its converse, and its contrapositive, with a justification or counterexample for each.
rubric: If-then form: for all real x, if x² > 4 then x > 2
Statement false: counterexample x = −3
Converse (if x > 2 then x² > 4) true: x > 2 > 0 gives x² > 4
Contrapositive (if x ≤ 2 then x² ≤ 4) false, same counterexample x = −3, consistent with equivalence
exam.why: "\( P \) only if \( Q \)" is \( P \to Q \). A counterexample to a universal conditional is a single value making the hypothesis true and the conclusion false.

exam.model:
Invalid. Search for rows with \( R = \) F and both premises true. \( P \to R \) true with \( R = \) F forces \( P = \) F. Then \( P \vee Q \) true forces \( Q = \) T. So the only bad row is \( P = \) F, \( Q = \) T, \( R = \) F, where \( P \vee Q \) is T, \( P \to R \) is T (vacuously) and \( R \) is F.

Adding the premise \( Q \to R \) makes it valid: premises \( P \vee Q \), \( P \to R \), \( Q \to R \) with conclusion \( R \) is proof by cases. (Adding \( \neg Q \) also works, via disjunctive syllogism and modus ponens.)
exam.prompt: Determine whether the argument with premises \( P \vee Q \) and \( P \to R \) and conclusion \( R \) is valid. If it is invalid, give every assignment of truth values that shows this. Then state one additional premise that would make it valid, and name the resulting rule.
rubric: Declares the argument invalid
Finds the unique bad row P = F, Q = T, R = F
Verifies premises true and conclusion false in that row
Adds Q → R, giving proof by cases (or another correct fix such as ¬Q)
exam.why: Systematic search for a falsifying row either finds all of them or shows none exists. Here exactly one row falsifies the argument, and \( Q \to R \) is exactly the premise that rules it out.

mth-6-0.intro:
Every proof you will write is a chain of claims, each of which must follow from earlier ones. Whether a step really follows is often invisible in ordinary English: "if", "only if", "or" and "not all" are used loosely in conversation, and a loose reading of any one of them is enough to turn a valid argument into an invalid one. Mathematics therefore needs a precise account of how the truth of a compound claim depends on the truth of its parts, and a mechanical test for when two claims say the same thing.

**Propositional logic** supplies that account for claims built from "and", "or", "not", "if…then" and "if and only if"; **predicate logic** extends it to claims about "all" and "some". This chapter develops both far enough to do three jobs you will need constantly in the rest of the course: read a theorem's logical form correctly, write the exact negation of a statement, and check whether an argument is valid.

rules.example: \( (2 + 2 = 5) \to Q \) is true for any \( Q \).
rules.formula: \( P \to Q \) is false only when \( P \) is T and \( Q \) is F
rules.name: Conditional truth table
rules.watch: A false hypothesis makes the conditional true, not undefined.
rules.when: Evaluating any if-then statement, especially with a false hypothesis.

rules.example: 'Differentiable only if continuous' is differentiable \( \to \) continuous.
rules.formula: '\( P \) only if \( Q \)', '\( Q \) necessary for \( P \)', '\( P \) sufficient for \( Q \)' all mean \( P \to Q \)
rules.name: Only if / necessary / sufficient
rules.watch: The 'if' in 'only if' does not mark the hypothesis.
rules.when: Translating English theorem statements.

rules.example: 'If \( n^{2} \) even then \( n \) even' is equivalent to 'if \( n \) odd then \( n^{2} \) odd'.
rules.formula: \( P \to Q \equiv \neg Q \to \neg P \)
rules.name: Contrapositive
rules.watch: The converse \( Q \to P \) is not equivalent.
rules.when: Rewriting a conditional into a more convenient equivalent form.

rules.example: Not (even and prime) \( \equiv \) odd or not prime.
rules.formula:
\( 
eg (P \wedge Q) \equiv 
eg P \vee 
eg Q \), \( 
eg (P \vee Q) \equiv 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q \)
rules.name: De Morgan
rules.watch: The connective must swap.
rules.when: Negating 'and' or 'or'.

rules.example: Not (if converges then terms \( \to 0 \)) \( \equiv \) converges and terms do not \( \to 0 \).
rules.formula: \( \neg (P \to Q) \equiv P \wedge \neg Q \)
rules.name: Negated conditional
rules.watch: It is a conjunction, never \( P \to \neg Q \).
rules.when: Negating an if-then, e.g. to set up a proof by contradiction or a counterexample.

rules.formula: \( P \to Q \equiv \neg P \vee Q \)
rules.name: Conditional as disjunction
rules.watch: Convert all conditionals first, simplify, then convert back.
rules.when: Simplifying formulas algebraically.

rules.formula:
\( 
eg  orall x\,P(x) \equiv \exists x\,
eg P(x) \), \( 
eg \exists x\,P(x) \equiv  orall x\,
eg P(x) \)
rules.name: Quantifier negation
rules.watch: Restrictions like \( \varepsilon > 0 \) are not negated.
rules.when: Negating any quantified statement, left to right.

rules.example: 'Some prime is even': \( \exists p\,(p \text{ prime} \wedge p \text{ even}) \).
rules.formula: \( \forall x \in A\,P(x) \equiv \forall x\,(x \in A \to P(x)) \); \( \exists x \in A\,P(x) \equiv \exists x\,(x \in A \wedge P(x)) \)
rules.name: Restricted quantifiers
rules.watch: Never \( \exists x\,(x \in A \to P(x)) \).
rules.when: Translating between restricted and unrestricted forms.

rules.example: \( P \to Q, Q \therefore P \) fails at \( P = \) F, \( Q = \) T.
rules.formula: Valid iff no assignment makes all premises T and the conclusion F
rules.name: Validity test
rules.watch: Validity is about form; a valid argument can have a false conclusion if a premise is false.
rules.when: Checking any argument or proof step.

stuck: To test a claimed equivalence quickly, hunt for one row where the two sides differ; if the search fails in every case, the formulas are equivalent.
Before negating, ask: what exact situation makes the original false? Your negation must describe exactly that.
Convert every conditional to a disjunction, simplify with De Morgan and distributivity, then convert back.
For nested quantifiers, read left to right as a game: \( \forall \) is the opponent's choice, \( \exists \) is your reply, and your reply may depend on earlier choices.
To check an argument, assume the conclusion false and all premises true, and propagate forced values until you reach a contradiction or a bad row.

kps.d: Decide whether a sentence is a statement, distinguishing unknown truth value from no truth value.
Give the truth tables of ¬, ∧, ∨ (inclusive), and translate English 'and/but/or/neither' correctly.
State the truth table of P → Q and justify the rows with false hypothesis.
Translate 'only if', 'necessary', 'sufficient', 'whenever' into P → Q with the correct direction.
Form the three related conditionals and know which are equivalent to the original.
Use P ↔ Q, its truth table, and its decomposition into two conditionals.
Build a complete 2ⁿ-row truth table systematically, subformula by subformula.
Classify formulas and decide equivalence or non-equivalence using tables or a falsifying row.
Apply De Morgan, distributive, conditional-as-disjunction and negated-conditional laws to transform and negate formulas.
Read, write and evaluate quantified statements, including restricted and nested quantifiers where order matters.
Push a negation through several quantifiers and a quantifier-free matrix correctly.
Test validity, apply modus ponens/tollens and related rules, and recognize the two classic fallacies.

practice.model:
Two variables give \( 2^{2} = 4 \) rows.

| \( P \) | \( Q \) | \( \neg Q \) | \( P \leftrightarrow \neg Q \) | \( P \leftrightarrow Q \) | \( \neg (P \leftrightarrow Q) \) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | F | T | F |
| T | F | T | T | F | T |
| F | T | F | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | F | T | F |

The fourth and sixth columns agree in every row, so the formulas are equivalent. Both say that \( P \) and \( Q \) have different truth values (exclusive or).
practice.prompt: Construct a complete truth table to decide whether \( P \leftrightarrow \neg Q \) and \( \neg (P \leftrightarrow Q) \) are logically equivalent. State how many rows are needed and why.
rubric: Four rows because there are 2 variables (2² assignments)
Correct columns for ¬Q, P ↔ ¬Q, P ↔ Q, ¬(P ↔ Q)
Final columns agree in every row: F, T, T, F
Concludes they are equivalent
practice.why: Equivalence requires agreement in all \( 2^{n} \) rows.

practice.model:
\( P \leftrightarrow Q \equiv (P \wedge Q) \vee (
eg P \wedge 
eg Q) \). The biconditional is true exactly when \( P \) and \( Q \) are both true or both false. The first disjunct is true exactly in the row where both are true, the second exactly in the row where both are false, so the disjunction is true in exactly those two rows and false in the other two, matching \( P \leftrightarrow Q \). (Alternatively, from \( (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P) \) and conditional-as-disjunction: \( (
eg P \vee Q) \wedge (
eg Q \vee P) \).)
practice.prompt: Express \( P \leftrightarrow Q \) using only \( \neg \), \( \wedge \), \( \vee \), and justify your answer by describing exactly when each side is true.
rubric: Answer (P ∧ Q) ∨ (¬P ∧ ¬Q) (or an equivalent such as (¬P ∨ Q) ∧ (P ∨ ¬Q))
P ↔ Q true exactly when P, Q have the same value
The disjunction is true exactly in the TT and FF rows
Concludes the two agree in every row
practice.why: Describe the true rows of the target and write one conjunction for each; their disjunction is an equivalent formula (disjunctive normal form).

practice.model:
"\( P \) only if \( Q \)" is \( P \to Q \): "If you may enroll in MHF 3302, then you have passed MAC 2311."

Contrapositive: "If you have not passed MAC 2311, then you may not enroll in MHF 3302." This is equivalent to the original.

Converse: "If you have passed MAC 2311, then you may enroll in MHF 3302." This is not equivalent: the original states a necessary condition for enrolling, not a sufficient one; there could be other requirements.
practice.prompt: Rewrite "You may enroll in MHF 3302 only if you have passed MAC 2311" as an if-then sentence. Then write its contrapositive and its converse in English, and say which of the two is equivalent to the original.
rubric: If-then form: if you may enroll in MHF 3302, then you have passed MAC 2311
Contrapositive: if you have not passed MAC 2311, then you may not enroll
Converse: if you have passed MAC 2311, then you may enroll
Only the contrapositive is equivalent to the original
practice.why: "Only if" introduces the conclusion (the necessary condition), not the hypothesis.

practice.model:
The hypothesis \( 2 + 2 = 5 \) is false, and a conditional with a false hypothesis is true by definition (vacuous truth), whatever the conclusion.

The reason for the definition: take the theorem "for every integer \( n \), if \( n \) is divisible by 4 then \( n \) is even". For it to be true, the conditional must be true for every integer. At \( n = 6 \) the hypothesis is false and conclusion true; at \( n = 3 \) both are false. If a conditional with a false hypothesis were declared false, this obviously correct theorem would be false. So the rows with false hypothesis must be true: a conditional only makes a claim about cases where its hypothesis holds.
practice.prompt: Explain why the sentence "If \( 2 + 2 = 5 \), then every prime is even" is true under the mathematical definition of the conditional, and explain why mathematics adopts that definition, using a general theorem of the form \( \forall n\, (P(n) \to Q(n)) \) as your illustration.
rubric: Hypothesis is false, so the conditional is (vacuously) true by the truth table
A universal conditional theorem must be true at every n, including those where P(n) is false
Concrete illustration, e.g. 'if n is divisible by 4 then n is even' at n = 3 or n = 6
Concludes the F-hypothesis rows must be T for such theorems to be true
practice.why: The truth table of \( \to \) is forced by the requirement that universal conditionals behave correctly across all instances.

practice.model:
\( \neg \forall x\, \exists n\ (n > x) \equiv \exists x\, \forall n\ (n \le x) \): "some real number is greater than or equal to every natural number."

The original is true (the Archimedean property): given real \( x \), if \( x < 1 \) take \( n = 1 \); otherwise take \( n = \lfloor x \rfloor + 1 \), which is a natural number greater than \( x \). Hence the negation, which says \( \mathbb{N} \) is bounded above in \( \mathbb{R} \), is false.
practice.prompt: Let the domain of \( x \) be \( \mathbb{R} \) and of \( n \) be \( \mathbb{N} \). Negate \( \forall x\, \exists n\ (n > x) \), pushing the negation all the way in. State which of the original and its negation is true, with a reason.
rubric: Negation: ∃x ∀n (n ≤ x)
Both quantifiers switched and > becomes ≤
Original is true: for any real x, a natural number larger than x exists (e.g. ⌊x⌋ + 1 when x ≥ 0, or 1 when x < 0; Archimedean property)
Therefore the negation (a real upper bound for ℕ) is false
practice.why: Exactly one of a statement and its negation is true.

practice.model:
\[ (P \wedge Q) 	o R \equiv 
eg (P \wedge Q) \vee R \equiv 
eg P \vee 
eg Q \vee R. \]
\[ (P 	o R) \vee (Q 	o R) \equiv (
eg P \vee R) \vee (
eg Q \vee R) \equiv 
eg P \vee 
eg Q \vee (R \vee R) \equiv 
eg P \vee 
eg Q \vee R. \]
They are equivalent. In words: "\( P \) and \( Q \) together imply \( R \)" says the same as "\( P \) alone implies \( R \), or \( Q \) alone implies \( R \)". This is surprising at first, because it compares with \( (P \vee Q) 	o R \equiv (P 	o R) \wedge (Q 	o R) \), where the connectives swap the other way.
practice.prompt: Is \( (P \wedge Q) \to R \) logically equivalent to \( (P \to R) \vee (Q \to R) \)? Decide using the laws of logic, and state the result in words.
rubric: Converts left side to ¬(P ∧ Q) ∨ R
De Morgan: ¬P ∨ ¬Q ∨ R
Rewrites right side as (¬P ∨ R) ∨ (¬Q ∨ R) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q ∨ R (idempotence/commutativity/associativity)
Concludes they are equivalent, with interpretation
practice.why: Converting every conditional to a disjunction reduces both sides to \( \neg P \vee \neg Q \vee R \). A brute-force table over 8 rows confirms it.

practice.prompt: Which sentence is the negation of "Every student passed some exam"?
practice.why: The original is \( \forall s\, \exists e\ \text{Passed}(s, e) \). Its negation is \( \exists s\, \forall e\ \neg \text{Passed}(s, e) \): some student passed no exam. "No student passed any exam" turns "not all" into "none". "Some student failed some exam" switches only the first quantifier. "Every student failed some exam" negates only the inner part.

eg Q \vee R \) and \( 
eg R \), disjunctive syllogism gives \( 
eg Q \). From \( P 	o Q \) and \( 
eg Q \), modus tollens gives \( 
eg P \). Every step is a valid rule, so the argument is valid. (Checking all 8 rows confirms that whenever the three premises are true, \( P \) is false.)

eg Q \vee R \), \( 
eg R \) and conclusion \( 
eg P \) is valid. Justify by naming the rules of inference you use, or by exhibiting a bad row.

From ¬R and ¬Q ∨ R derives ¬Q
From P → Q and ¬Q derives ¬P by modus tollens
Concludes valid

practice.prompt: How many rows does a complete truth table need for the formula \( \big( (P \to Q) \wedge (R \vee \neg S) \big) \leftrightarrow (T \wedge P) \)?
practice.why: The distinct variables are \( P, Q, R, S, T \): five of them. Each can be T or F independently, so there are \( 2^{5} = 32 \) assignments. Repeated occurrences of \( P \) do not add rows.

practice.model:
\( \forall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) \) is true: given any integer \( x \), \( y = x + 1 \) works.

\( \exists y\, \forall x\, (x < y) \) is false: it would require one integer \( y \) greater than every integer, but taking \( x = y \) gives \( y < y \), which is false.

In \( \forall x\, \exists y \), the witness \( y \) is chosen after \( x \) and may depend on it. In \( \exists y\, \forall x \), a single \( y \) must be fixed first and must work for all \( x \) simultaneously. The second form implies the first, but not conversely; here the first is true and the second false.
practice.prompt: Over the domain \( \mathbb{Z} \), decide the truth of \( \forall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) \) and \( \exists y\, \forall x\, (x < y) \). Explain precisely how swapping the quantifiers changes what is asserted.
rubric: First true: for each x take y = x + 1
Second false: any proposed y fails at x = y (y < y is false)
Explains in ∀x∃y, y may depend on x; in ∃y∀x, a single y must work for all x
Notes ∃y∀x implies ∀x∃y but not conversely
practice.why: Order of mixed quantifiers encodes dependence: \( \exists \) after \( \forall \) may depend on the \( \forall \) variable.

practice.model:
The converse is \( Q 	o P \); the inverse is \( 
eg P 	o 
eg Q \). The contrapositive of \( Q 	o P \) is \( 
eg P 	o 
eg Q \), and every conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive, so the converse and inverse are equivalent.

The converse is not equivalent to the original: at \( P = \) F, \( Q = \) T, \( P 	o Q \) is T but \( Q 	o P \) is F. So proving the inverse establishes the converse, which may be true while the original is false, or vice versa. It says nothing about \( P 	o Q \).
practice.prompt: Prove, by a truth table or by the laws of logic, that the converse and the inverse of \( P \to Q \) are logically equivalent to each other. Then explain why this means a proof of the inverse is not a proof of the original statement.
rubric: Converse Q → P and inverse ¬P → ¬Q
Shows equivalence: ¬P → ¬Q is the contrapositive of Q → P (or table)
Notes converse is not equivalent to the original (row P = F, Q = T)
Concludes proving the inverse proves the converse, not the original
practice.why: The four related conditionals fall into two equivalence classes: {original, contrapositive} and {converse, inverse}.

mth-6-0.scope: Propositional logic (connectives, truth tables, equivalence, laws, negation), predicate logic with nested quantifiers and their negation, and validity of arguments; proof methods themselves are left to the next topic.

sections.md:
This section answers a basic question: what kind of sentence can be the subject of a proof, and how are complicated claims built from simpler ones so that their truth can be computed?

> A **statement** (or **proposition**) is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both.

"7 is prime" is a statement (true). "\( 2^{10} < 1000 \)" is a statement (false, since \( 2^{10} = 1024 \)). "Every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two primes" (Goldbach's conjecture) is a statement even though nobody currently knows its truth value: what matters is that it has one. By contrast, "Is 7 prime?" is a question, "Prove the theorem" is a command, and "\( x + 1 = 5 \)" is not yet a statement, because its truth depends on the value of \( x \). Sentences of that last kind are handled in the section on quantifiers.

We abbreviate statements by letters \( P, Q, R, \dots \), called **propositional variables**, and combine them with **logical connectives**. The three basic ones are:

- **Negation** \( \neg P \) ("not \( P \)"): true exactly when \( P \) is false. (Hammack's *Book of Proof* writes \( \sim P \).)
- **Conjunction** \( P \wedge Q \) ("\( P \) and \( Q \)"): true exactly when both \( P \) and \( Q \) are true.
- **Disjunction** \( P \vee Q \) ("\( P \) or \( Q \)"): true exactly when at least one of \( P, Q \) is true.

These definitions are recorded in a **truth table**, which lists every possible assignment of truth values to the variables and the resulting value of the compound statement:

| \( P \) | \( Q \) | \( \neg P \) | \( P \wedge Q \) | \( P \vee Q \) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | T |
| F | T | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | F | F |

Two features deserve emphasis. First, the mathematical "or" is **inclusive**: \( P \vee Q \) is true when both parts are true. The **exclusive or**, "one or the other but not both", is a different connective, and when mathematicians mean it they say so explicitly. Second, each connective is **truth-functional**: the truth value of the compound depends only on the truth values of its parts, not on what the parts are about. That is what makes truth tables possible.

Several English words translate to the same connective. "But", "although" and "whereas" all become \( \wedge \): "\( 6 \) is even but not prime" is \( P \wedge \neg Q \). "Neither \( P \) nor \( Q \)" means \( \neg P \wedge \neg Q \).

**Worked example.** Let \( P \): "6 is even" (true) and \( Q \): "6 is prime" (false). Evaluate \( \neg (P \wedge Q) \) and \( \neg P \wedge \neg Q \).

1. \( P \wedge Q \) is T \( \wedge \) F, which is F. So \( \neg (P \wedge Q) \) is \( \neg \)F, which is T. In words: "6 is not both even and prime" is true.
2. \( \neg P \) is F and \( \neg Q \) is T, so \( \neg P \wedge \neg Q \) is F \( \wedge \) T, which is F. In words: "6 is neither even nor prime" is false.

The two formulas received different truth values from the same assignment, so they do not say the same thing.

**The common mistake** is to "distribute" a negation across a connective without changing the connective, reading "not both \( P \) and \( Q \)" as "not \( P \) and not \( Q \)". The worked example is a single assignment that refutes this. The correct rule (De Morgan's law, proved later) changes \( \wedge \) to \( \vee \): "not both" means "at least one fails". A second common mistake is treating an unknown truth value as no truth value. A statement need not be *known*; it must be *definite*.

questions.model:
(a) A statement; it is true, since \( 3^{4} = 81 \).

(b) Not a statement. It contains the variable \( x \) with no value assigned and no quantifier, so it is true for \( x = \pm 2 \) and false otherwise. It is an open sentence.

(c) A statement. It is a declarative sentence that is either true or false; which one is not currently known (it is the twin prime conjecture), but a statement only needs to have a definite truth value, not a known one.

(d) Not a statement. It is an instruction; it asserts nothing that could be true or false.

sections.title: Statements and the basic connectives

sections.md:
Almost every theorem has the form "if (hypotheses) then (conclusion)". This section fixes exactly what such a sentence asserts, and how to recognise the same logical form behind several different English phrasings.

> The **conditional** \( P \to Q \) ("if \( P \) then \( Q \)") is false when \( P \) is true and \( Q \) is false, and true in every other case. \( P \) is the **hypothesis** (or **antecedent**); \( Q \) is the **conclusion** (or **consequent**).

| \( P \) | \( Q \) | \( P \to Q \) |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | T |

(*Book of Proof* writes \( P \Rightarrow Q \).) The first two rows are uncontroversial. The last two, where the hypothesis is false, need justification. Consider the theorem "for every integer \( n \), if \( n \) is divisible by 4 then \( n \) is even". We certainly want this to be true, which means the conditional must be true for *every* integer \( n \). For \( n = 6 \), the hypothesis is false and the conclusion true (row 3); for \( n = 3 \), both are false (row 4). If either of those rows were F, the theorem would be false. So the truth table is forced on us by how mathematicians use conditionals inside general statements. A conditional whose hypothesis is false is said to be **vacuously true**: it makes no claim about that case.

**English forms.** All of the following mean \( P \to Q \):

- if \( P \), then \( Q \); \( Q \) if \( P \); \( Q \) whenever \( P \); \( P \) implies \( Q \);
- \( P \) **only if** \( Q \);
- \( P \) is **sufficient** for \( Q \); \( Q \) is **necessary** for \( P \).

"Only if" is the one that causes trouble. "\( P \) only if \( Q \)" says that \( P \) cannot happen without \( Q \), that is, whenever \( P \) holds, \( Q \) holds. The word "if" in "only if" does *not* mark the hypothesis. Similarly, a necessary condition is what the conclusion supplies: if \( P \to Q \), then \( Q \) is necessary for \( P \) because \( P \) cannot be true without it.

**Related conditionals.** From \( P \to Q \) we form:

- the **converse** \( Q \to P \);
- the **inverse** \( \neg P \to \neg Q \);
- the **contrapositive** \( \neg Q \to \neg P \).

The contrapositive always has the same truth value as the original (verified by truth table in the next section); the converse need not. For "if \( n \) is divisible by 4 then \( n \) is even", the statement is true, the contrapositive "if \( n \) is odd then \( n \) is not divisible by 4" is true, but the converse "if \( n \) is even then \( n \) is divisible by 4" is false (take \( n = 2 \)).

> The **biconditional** \( P \leftrightarrow Q \) ("\( P \) if and only if \( Q \)", abbreviated "\( P \) iff \( Q \)") is true when \( P \) and \( Q \) have the same truth value, and false otherwise.

"\( P \) if and only if \( Q \)" is literally "\( P \) if \( Q \)" (that is, \( Q \to P \)) together with "\( P \) only if \( Q \)" (that is, \( P \to Q \)). So \( P \leftrightarrow Q \) says the same as \( (P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to P) \), and "\( Q \) is necessary and sufficient for \( P \)" is another way to say it. A proof of an "iff" theorem therefore consists of two proofs, one for each direction.

**Worked example.** Rewrite "a real number \( x \) satisfies \( x^{2} = x \) only if \( x = 1 \)" in if-then form and decide its truth.

1. "\( P \) only if \( Q \)" is \( P \to Q \), with \( P \): \( x^{2} = x \) and \( Q \): \( x = 1 \). So: "if \( x^{2} = x \), then \( x = 1 \)".
2. The hypothesis \( x^{2} = x \) means \( x(x - 1) = 0 \), so \( x = 0 \) or \( x = 1 \). At \( x = 0 \) the hypothesis is true and the conclusion false, so the claim (read as "for all real \( x \)") is false.
3. Its converse, "if \( x = 1 \) then \( x^{2} = x \)", is true.

**The common mistakes** are assuming a conditional's converse (the most frequent logical error in proofs) and reading "\( P \) only if \( Q \)" as \( Q \to P \).

questions.model:
Converse: "If \( f \) is continuous at \( a \), then \( f \) is differentiable at \( a \)." False: \( f(x) = \lvert x \rvert \) is continuous at \( 0 \) but not differentiable there (the difference quotient has one-sided limits \( 1 \) and \( -1 \)).

Inverse: "If \( f \) is not differentiable at \( a \), then \( f \) is not continuous at \( a \)." False, by the same example: \( \lvert x \rvert \) is not differentiable at \( 0 \) yet is continuous there. (The inverse is the contrapositive of the converse, so it must fail whenever the converse does.)

Contrapositive: "If \( f \) is not continuous at \( a \), then \( f \) is not differentiable at \( a \)." True, because a contrapositive always has the same truth value as the original conditional, and the original is a theorem of calculus.

That is \( P \to Q \) (and here it is true: a multiple of 6 is even). Choosing \( Q \to P \) reads the sentence left to right; choosing \( P \leftrightarrow Q \) confuses "necessary" with "necessary and sufficient"; \( \neg P \to \neg Q \) is the inverse, which is equivalent to the converse \( Q \to P \), not to \( P \to Q \).

sections.title: The conditional and the biconditional

sections.md:
Once compound statements can be built, we need a reliable method for two questions: is a given formula true under every assignment, and do two formulas always agree? A complete truth table answers both mechanically.

**Building a truth table.** A formula with \( n \) distinct propositional variables has \( 2^{n} \) possible assignments, since each variable independently takes one of two values. List them systematically: in the first column, the top half T and the bottom half F; in the next, alternate in blocks of a quarter; and so on until the last column alternates T, F. Then add one column for each subformula, working from the innermost parentheses outward, so that every entry is computed from entries already in the table. The last column, for the **main connective**, gives the value of the whole formula.

> A **tautology** is a formula that is true under every assignment of truth values. A **contradiction** is a formula that is false under every assignment. A formula that is neither is a **contingency**.
>
> Two formulas \( A \) and \( B \) are **logically equivalent**, written \( A \equiv B \), if they have the same truth value under every assignment. Equivalently, \( A \leftrightarrow B \) is a tautology.

Note that \( \equiv \) is not a connective inside a formula; it is a claim *about* two formulas. \( P \vee \neg P \) is a tautology, and \( P \wedge \neg P \) is a contradiction.

**Worked example (equivalence).** Show that \( (P \vee Q) \to R \equiv (P \to R) \wedge (Q \to R) \). There are 3 variables, so \( 2^{3} = 8 \) rows.

| \( P \) | \( Q \) | \( R \) | \( P \vee Q \) | \( (P \vee Q) \to R \) | \( P \to R \) | \( Q \to R \) | \( (P \to R) \wedge (Q \to R) \) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | T | F | T | F | F | F | F |
| T | F | T | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | F | F | T | F |
| F | T | T | T | T | T | T | T |
| F | T | F | T | F | T | F | F |
| F | F | T | F | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | F | F | T | T | T | T |

Columns 5 and 8 agree in all eight rows, so the formulas are equivalent. This equivalence is the logical basis of **proof by cases**: to prove "if \( P \) or \( Q \), then \( R \)", prove \( P \to R \) and \( Q \to R \) separately.

**Worked example (contrapositive).** A four-row table for \( P \to Q \) and \( \neg Q \to \neg P \):

| \( P \) | \( Q \) | \( \neg Q \) | \( \neg P \) | \( P \to Q \) | \( \neg Q \to \neg P \) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | F | T | T |
| T | F | T | F | F | F |
| F | T | F | T | T | T |
| F | F | T | T | T | T |

The last two columns agree, so \( P \to Q \equiv \neg Q \to \neg P \). This is the justification for proof by contraposition in the next chapter.

**Proving non-equivalence.** To show two formulas are *not* equivalent, a single row suffices. For example, \( (P \to Q) \to R \) and \( P \to (Q \to R) \) differ at \( P = \) F, \( Q = \) T, \( R = \) F: the first is \( (\text{F} \to \text{T}) \to \text{F} \), that is T \( \to \) F, which is F; the second is F \( \to (\cdots) \), which is T. So \( \to \) is not associative, and the parentheses in a conditional matter.

**The common mistakes** are an incomplete table (fewer than \( 2^{n} \) rows, often from listing assignments unsystematically) and concluding equivalence from agreement on a few rows. Agreement must hold in every row; disagreement in one row settles non-equivalence.

| \( P \) | \( Q \) | \( P \to Q \) | \( Q \to P \) | \( (P \to Q) \vee (Q \to P) \) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | T |
| F | T | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | T | T |

Every row is T, so the formula is a tautology. Without the table: if \( Q \) is true, then \( P \to Q \) is true because its conclusion is true; if \( Q \) is false, then \( Q \to P \) is true because its hypothesis is false. Either way one disjunct is true.

sections.title: Truth tables, tautologies and logical equivalence

sections.md:
Truth tables grow as \( 2^{n} \), and they tell you *that* two formulas are equivalent without helping you transform one into the other. In proofs you constantly need to rewrite a statement into a more useful form, above all to write its negation. This section collects the standard equivalences, each checkable by a truth table, and uses them as algebraic rules.

sections.title: Laws of logic and negating compound statements

sections.md:
Propositional logic treats "\( x^{2} \ge 0 \)" as an indivisible block, but nearly every theorem is about *all* numbers of some kind, or asserts that *some* object exists. This section introduces the language needed to state such claims precisely.

> An **open sentence** (or **predicate**) \( P(x) \) is a sentence containing a variable \( x \) that becomes a statement whenever a specific object from a stated set, the **domain** (or **universe of discourse**), is substituted for \( x \).

"\( x^{2} = 4 \)" with domain \( \mathbb{R} \) is an open sentence: \( P(2) \) is true, \( P(3) \) is false. There are two ways to turn it into a statement without choosing a value: quantify it.

> The **universal quantifier**: \( \forall x\, P(x) \) ("for all \( x \), \( P(x) \)") is true if \( P(a) \) is true for every \( a \) in the domain, and false otherwise.
>
> The **existential quantifier**: \( \exists x\, P(x) \) ("there exists \( x \) such that \( P(x) \)") is true if \( P(a) \) is true for at least one \( a \) in the domain, and false otherwise.

A variable governed by a quantifier is **bound**; one that is not is **free**. A formula with no free variables is a statement.

**The domain is part of the meaning.** \( \exists x\, (x^{2} = 2) \) is true with domain \( \mathbb{R} \) (take \( x = \sqrt{2} \)) and false with domain \( \mathbb{Q} \). When the domain is not the whole universe under discussion, we write **restricted quantifiers**:
\[ \forall x \in A\ P(x) \ \text{ means } \ \forall x\, (x \in A \to P(x)), \qquad \exists x \in A\ P(x) \ \text{ means } \ \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge P(x)). \]
The connectives differ, and for a reason: a universal claim restricted to \( A \) says nothing about objects outside \( A \) (vacuously true there), while an existential claim needs a witness that is in \( A \) *and* has the property. Writing \( \exists x\, (x \in A \to P(x)) \) is a classic error: it is true as soon as some object lies outside \( A \).

**How to establish or refute each.** To prove \( \forall x\, P(x) \), you must argue about an arbitrary element; checking examples proves nothing. To refute it, one **counterexample** (an \( a \) with \( P(a) \) false) suffices. To prove \( \exists x\, P(x) \), one witness suffices; to refute it, you must show \( P(a) \) fails for every \( a \).

**Hidden quantifiers.** English often leaves quantifiers implicit. "The square of a real number is nonnegative" is \( \forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ (x^{2} \ge 0) \). "If \( n \) is divisible by 4, then \( n \) is even", stated as a theorem, carries an implicit \( \forall n \in \mathbb{Z} \).

**Nested quantifiers.** Many definitions use several quantifiers, and their **order matters**. Over the domain \( \mathbb{Z} \), compare
\[ \forall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \exists y\, \forall x\, (x + y = 0). \]

1. The first says: for each integer \( x \), some integer \( y \) satisfies \( x + y = 0 \). Given \( x \), take \( y = -x \). True. Note that \( y \) is chosen *after* \( x \) and may depend on it.
2. The second says: a single integer \( y \) works for every \( x \) simultaneously. If such \( y \) existed, then \( x = 0 \) gives \( y = 0 \), and \( x = 1 \) gives \( 1 + y = 1 \neq 0 \). False.

Read nested quantifiers left to right as a game: each \( \forall \) is a choice made by an opponent, each \( \exists \) is your reply, and later choices may depend on all earlier ones. Quantifiers of the same kind may be swapped freely: \( \forall x\, \forall y \) means the same as \( \forall y\, \forall x \).

**The common mistakes** are swapping \( \forall \exists \) to \( \exists \forall \) (which usually strengthens the claim enormously), and ignoring the domain.

sections.title: Predicates and quantifiers

sections.md:
Proof by contradiction begins by assuming the negation of what you want; disproving a claim means proving its negation. Both require writing negations of quantified statements correctly, often with three or four nested quantifiers. This section gives a mechanical procedure.

> **Negation of quantifiers.** For any open sentence \( P(x) \):
> \[ \neg \forall x\, P(x) \equiv \exists x\, \neg P(x), \qquad \neg \exists x\, P(x) \equiv \forall x\, \neg P(x). \]

The reasoning is direct. "Not every \( x \) has property \( P \)" means some \( x \) lacks it; this is exactly what a counterexample is. "No \( x \) has property \( P \)" means every \( x \) lacks it. These are De Morgan's laws in quantified form: \( \forall \) behaves like a (possibly infinite) conjunction over the domain and \( \exists \) like a disjunction.

For restricted quantifiers, the restriction stays unchanged:
\[ \neg \forall x \in A\ P(x) \equiv \exists x \in A\ \neg P(x), \qquad \neg \exists x \in A\ P(x) \equiv \forall x \in A\ \neg P(x). \]
To see this, expand: \( \neg \forall x\, (x \in A \to P(x)) \equiv \exists x\, \neg (x \in A \to P(x)) \equiv \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge \neg P(x)) \).

**Procedure.** Move the negation inward from left to right. Each time it passes a quantifier, switch \( \forall \) and \( \exists \), leaving the restriction alone. When it reaches the quantifier-free part, negate that using the propositional laws (De Morgan; \( \neg (A \to B) \equiv A \wedge \neg B \); \( \neg (a < b) \equiv a \ge b \)).

**Worked example.** A sequence \( (a_{n}) \) converges to \( L \) if
\[ \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists N \in \mathbb{N}\ \forall n \ge N\ \ \lvert a_{n} - L \rvert < \varepsilon. \]
Negate it to obtain the definition of "\( (a_{n}) \) does not converge to \( L \)".

1. \( \neg \forall \varepsilon > 0 \cdots \) becomes \( \exists \varepsilon > 0\ \neg (\cdots) \).
2. \( \neg \exists N \in \mathbb{N} \cdots \) becomes \( \forall N \in \mathbb{N}\ \neg (\cdots) \).
3. \( \neg \forall n \ge N \cdots \) becomes \( \exists n \ge N\ \neg (\cdots) \).
4. \( \neg \big( \lvert a_{n} - L \rvert < \varepsilon \big) \) becomes \( \lvert a_{n} - L \rvert \ge \varepsilon \).

Result:
\[ \exists \varepsilon > 0\ \forall N \in \mathbb{N}\ \exists n \ge N\ \ \lvert a_{n} - L \rvert \ge \varepsilon. \]
In words: there is a tolerance \( \varepsilon \) such that, however far out you go, some later term is at least \( \varepsilon \) away from \( L \). Notice that the restrictions \( \varepsilon > 0 \) and \( n \ge N \) were not negated. Negating \( \varepsilon > 0 \) to \( \varepsilon \le 0 \) would produce a statement about nonpositive tolerances, which is meaningless for the purpose.

**Worked example (with a conditional inside).** Negate "every prime greater than 2 is odd": \( \forall p\, \big( (p \text{ prime} \wedge p > 2) \to p \text{ odd} \big) \). The negation is \( \exists p\, \big( p \text{ prime} \wedge p > 2 \wedge p \text{ even} \big) \): "some prime greater than 2 is even". The conditional became a conjunction, as it must.

**The common mistakes**: turning "not all" into "none" (\( \neg \forall x\, P(x) \) is not \( \forall x\, \neg P(x) \)); negating the restriction on a quantified variable; forgetting to switch every quantifier; and leaving a conditional inside the negation as a conditional.

sections.title: Negating quantified statements

sections.md:
A proof is a sequence of inferences. This section makes precise when an inference is logically acceptable, and names the patterns you will use (and the ones you must avoid).

> An **argument** consists of statements called **premises** and a statement called the **conclusion**. The argument is **valid** if, under every assignment of truth values to the variables that makes all the premises true, the conclusion is also true. Equivalently, the conditional \( (\text{premise}_{1} \wedge \cdots \wedge \text{premise}_{k}) \to \text{conclusion} \) is a tautology.

Validity is about form, not content. A valid argument with a false premise may have a false conclusion; an argument is **sound** if it is valid *and* its premises are true, and only then is its conclusion guaranteed true. To test validity with a truth table, look only at the rows where every premise is T. The argument is valid exactly when the conclusion is T in all such rows. A single row with all premises T and the conclusion F shows the argument is **invalid**.

**Standard valid forms (rules of inference).**

| Name | Premises | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| **Modus ponens** | \( P \to Q \), \( P \) | \( Q \) |
| **Modus tollens** | \( P \to Q \), \( \neg Q \) | \( \neg P \) |
| Hypothetical syllogism | \( P \to Q \), \( Q \to R \) | \( P \to R \) |
| Disjunctive syllogism | \( P \vee Q \), \( \neg P \) | \( Q \) |
| Proof by cases | \( P \vee Q \), \( P \to R \), \( Q \to R \) | \( R \) |

Modus tollens is the contrapositive at work: from \( P \to Q \) we have \( \neg Q \to \neg P \), and modus ponens applies.

**Two fallacies.** These look similar to valid forms and are invalid:

- **Affirming the consequent**: \( P \to Q \), \( Q \), therefore \( P \). The row \( P = \) F, \( Q = \) T makes both premises true and the conclusion false.
- **Denying the antecedent**: \( P \to Q \), \( \neg P \), therefore \( \neg Q \). The same row refutes it.

Both are the error of assuming the converse.

**Worked example.** Decide whether the argument with premises \( P \to Q \), \( Q \to R \), \( \neg R \) and conclusion \( \neg P \) is valid.

1. Chain method: from \( Q \to R \) and \( \neg R \), modus tollens gives \( \neg Q \). From \( P \to Q \) and \( \neg Q \), modus tollens gives \( \neg P \). Each step is valid, so the argument is valid.
2. Truth-table check: the premises are all true only when \( R \) is F (third premise), then \( Q \) must be F (else \( Q \to R \) fails), then \( P \) must be F (else \( P \to Q \) fails). The only such row has \( P \) false, so the conclusion \( \neg P \) holds.

**Quantified forms.** The rules extend to predicates. **Universal instantiation** lets you apply \( \forall x\, P(x) \) to any particular element \( a \), giving \( P(a) \); combined with modus ponens: from \( \forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x)) \) and \( P(a) \), conclude \( Q(a) \). This is what happens every time you apply a theorem to a specific case.

**The common mistake** in proofs is affirming the consequent in disguise: proving that the desired conclusion implies something true, and then claiming the conclusion. For instance, "if \( \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} < 4 \) then (squaring) \( 5 + 2\sqrt{6} < 16 \), which is true, so the inequality holds" is invalid as written; the reasoning must run from known facts to the conclusion, or each step must be reversible and the reversal stated.

questions.model: With \( P \): "\( f \) is differentiable at \( 0 \)" and \( Q \): "\( f \) is continuous at \( 0 \)", the argument is \( P \to Q \), \( Q \), therefore \( P \): affirming the consequent. It is invalid. Under the assignment \( P = \) F, \( Q = \) T, both premises are true (the conditional is vacuously true) and the conclusion \( P \) is false. Concretely, \( f(x) = \lvert x \rvert \) is continuous at \( 0 \), the conditional premise is a true theorem, and yet \( f \) is not differentiable at \( 0 \).
questions.prompt: Assess the argument: "If \( f \) is differentiable at \( 0 \), then \( f \) is continuous at \( 0 \). The function \( f \) is continuous at \( 0 \). Therefore \( f \) is differentiable at \( 0 \)." Name its form, state whether it is valid, and support your verdict both with a truth-value assignment and with a concrete function.

States it is invalid
Gives the assignment P = F, Q = T making both premises true and conclusion false

questions.why: An argument is invalid if some assignment makes all premises true and the conclusion false. Affirming the consequent treats \( P \to Q \) as if it were \( Q \to P \).

questions.model:
Suppose some assignment makes \( P \vee Q \), \( P \to R \), \( Q \to R \) true and \( R \) false. Since \( P \to R \) is true and \( R \) is false, \( P \) must be false; likewise \( Q \to R \) true and \( R \) false force \( Q \) false. Then \( P \vee Q \) is false, contradicting the first premise. So no such assignment exists and the argument is valid (it is proof by cases).

Dropping the premise \( Q \to R \) breaks it: at \( P = \) F, \( Q = \) T, \( R = \) F, the premises \( P \vee Q \) (T) and \( P \to R \) (vacuously T) are true while \( R \) is false. So that argument is invalid.

q is some p_i, so q divides both N and p₁⋯p_k, hence q | 1
Contradiction: no prime divides 1 (primes exceed 1); does not claim N itself is prime
exam.why: The contradiction is "\( q \mid 1 \)" with \( q > 1 \). The argument does not need \( N \) to be prime, and \( N \) often is not (\( 30031 = 59 \cdot 509 \)).

exam.model: *Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, \( \sqrt{6} = \frac{a}{b} \) with integers \( a, b \), \( b \neq 0 \), not both even (lowest terms). Then \( a^{2} = 6b^{2} = 2(3b^{2}) \) is even, so \( a \) is even: \( a = 2c \). Substituting, \( 4c^{2} = 6b^{2} \), so \( 3b^{2} = 2c^{2} \) is even. If \( b \) were odd, \( b^{2} \) would be odd and so \( 3b^{2} \) would be odd (a product of odd integers); hence \( b \) is even. Now \( a \) and \( b \) are both even, a contradiction. \( \blacksquare \)
exam.prompt: Prove that \( \sqrt{6} \) is irrational. You may use the lemma "if \( n^{2} \) is even then \( n \) is even".
rubric: Assumes √6 = a/b in lowest terms and derives a² = 6b²
a² even, so a even, a = 2c, giving 4c² = 6b², i.e. 2c² = 3b²
3b² even forces b even (if b odd, 3b² odd)
Both a, b even contradicts lowest terms
exam.why: The \( \sqrt{2} \) template works with one extra parity step: \( 3b^{2} \) even forces \( b \) even.

exam.model: The statement is false. Take \( a = 1 \), \( b = -1 \). Then \( a \mid b \) because \( -1 = 1 \cdot (-1) \), and \( b \mid a \) because \( 1 = (-1)(-1) \). But \( a \neq b \). (What is true is that \( a = \pm b \); the statement becomes true if \( a \) and \( b \) are restricted to positive integers.)
exam.prompt: Prove or disprove: for all integers \( a \) and \( b \), if \( a \mid b \) and \( b \mid a \), then \( a = b \).
rubric: Declares the statement false
Counterexample a = 1, b = −1 (or a = 2, b = −2)
Verifies both divisibilities: −1 = 1·(−1) and 1 = (−1)(−1)
Notes a ≠ b; optionally that the true statement is a = ±b
exam.why: Test extreme and sign-changing cases first; negatives often break statements that are true for natural numbers.

exam.model:
(a) *Case \( n = 2k \):* \( n^{2} + n = 4k^{2} + 2k = 2(2k^{2} + k) \). *Case \( n = 2k + 1 \):* \( n^{2} + n = 4k^{2} + 4k + 1 + 2k + 1 = 4k^{2} + 6k + 2 = 2(2k^{2} + 3k + 1) \). Both even; the cases are exhaustive.

(b) \( n^{2} + n = n(n + 1) \). Of the consecutive integers \( n \) and \( n + 1 \), one is even (if \( n \) is odd, \( n + 1 \) is even), and a product with an even factor is even.

The factorization proof generalizes more easily: the same idea shows that a product of \( k \) consecutive integers is divisible by \( k \) (one of them is a multiple of \( k \)), e.g. \( 3 \mid n(n + 1)(n + 2) \), whereas the expansion-by-cases approach grows messier with each new case. Note that (b) still rests on a small case split to justify "one of two consecutive integers is even".
exam.prompt: Prove that for every integer \( n \), \( n^{2} + n \) is even, (a) by cases on the parity of \( n \), and (b) by a single direct argument that uses a factorization. Which proof generalizes more easily, and why?
rubric: (a) Case n = 2k: n² + n = 2(2k² + k); case n = 2k + 1: n² + n = 4k² + 6k + 2 = 2(2k² + 3k + 1)
(b) n² + n = n(n + 1), a product of consecutive integers, one of which is even
(b) justifies that one of n, n + 1 is even (if n is odd, n + 1 is even), which is itself a small parity case split
Reasoned comment on generalization, e.g. n(n + 1)(n + 2) divisible by 6 follows the factor-based idea
exam.why: Both are valid; structural arguments (factor, then use a general fact) tend to extend further than computation.

exam.model:
*Existence.* Let \( x = -\frac{b}{a} \), which is defined because \( a \neq 0 \). Then \( a\left(-\frac{b}{a}\right) + b = -b + b = 0 \).

*Uniqueness.* Suppose \( ax_{1} + b = 0 \) and \( ax_{2} + b = 0 \). Subtracting, \( a(x_{1} - x_{2}) = 0 \). Since \( a \neq 0 \), dividing by \( a \) gives \( x_{1} - x_{2} = 0 \), so \( x_{1} = x_{2} \). \( \blacksquare \)

The hypothesis \( a \neq 0 \) is used twice: to define the solution and to cancel \( a \) in the uniqueness step. (If \( a = 0 \), there is no solution when \( b \neq 0 \) and every real is a solution when \( b = 0 \).)
exam.prompt: Prove that for every real number \( a \neq 0 \) and every real \( b \), the equation \( ax + b = 0 \) has exactly one real solution. Identify the existence and uniqueness parts, and point out where \( a \neq 0 \) is used.
rubric: Existence: x = −b/a, verified by substitution (uses a ≠ 0 to divide)
Uniqueness: suppose ax₁ + b = 0 and ax₂ + b = 0
Subtracts to get a(x₁ − x₂) = 0 and uses a ≠ 0 to conclude x₁ = x₂
Clearly labels both parts
exam.why: Existence and uniqueness are separate claims, each needing its own argument.

mth-6-1.intro:
Checking a claim on many examples, however many, does not establish it. The polynomial \( n^{2} + n + 41 \) is prime for \( n = 0, 1, 2, \dots, 39 \), and then \( 40^{2} + 40 + 41 = 41^{2} \). A **proof** is what closes that gap: a finite chain of statements, each justified by definitions, previously proved results or valid rules of inference, ending in the claim, so that the claim holds in *every* case covered by its hypotheses.

The logic of the previous topic tells you what a statement means and what counts as a valid inference; it does not tell you how to find a proof. This topic supplies the standard strategies: the direct proof, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, proof by cases, proofs of biconditionals, existence and uniqueness proofs, and disproof by counterexample. Each is chosen by looking at the logical form of what you must prove, which is why the logic comes first.

rules.example: Given \( a \mid b \): write \( b = ak \). Goal \( a \mid c \): find \( m \) with \( c = am \).
rules.formula: even: \( n = 2k \); odd: \( n = 2k + 1 \); \( a \mid b \): \( b = ac \); rational: \( x = a/b,\ b \neq 0 \)
rules.name: Unfold definitions
rules.watch: Use a fresh letter for each hypothesis.
rules.when: At the start of every proof about integers or rationals.

rules.example: \( m, n \) odd \( \Rightarrow m + n = 2(k + l + 1) \).
rules.formula: Assume \( P \); deduce \( Q \)
rules.name: Direct proof
rules.watch: Scratch work may run backward; the write-up must run forward.
rules.when: The hypothesis unpacks into something you can compute with.

rules.example: \( n^{2} \) even \( \Rightarrow n \) even: assume \( n = 2k + 1 \), get \( n^{2} \) odd.
rules.formula: Assume \( \neg Q \); deduce \( \neg P \)
rules.name: Contrapositive
rules.watch: Negate 'or' as 'and' (De Morgan); do not prove the converse.
rules.when: The negated conclusion is more concrete than the hypothesis.

rules.example: \( \sqrt{2} = a/b \) in lowest terms forces \( a, b \) both even.
rules.formula:
Assume \( 
eg P \) (or \( P \wedge 
eg Q \)); derive \( C \wedge 
eg C \)
rules.name: Contradiction
rules.watch: The contradiction must be genuine; set up lowest terms or minimality before you need it.
rules.when: Negative statements (irrational, no largest, infinitely many) or no usable hypothesis.

rules.formula: \( P_{1} \vee \cdots \vee P_{k} \), each \( P_{i} \to Q \), therefore \( Q \)
rules.name: Cases
rules.watch: Cases must be exhaustive; WLOG only for true symmetry.
rules.when: The hypothesis or domain splits naturally (parity, remainders, sign).

rules.example: \( n \) even iff \( n^{2} \) even: direct one way, contrapositive the other.
rules.formula: Prove \( P \to Q \) and \( Q \to P \)
rules.name: Biconditional
rules.watch: Both directions are required.
rules.when: Statements with 'if and only if' or 'necessary and sufficient'.

rules.formula: Exhibit \( a \) with \( P(a) \); then \( P(y) \wedge P(z) \Rightarrow y = z \)
rules.name: Existence and uniqueness
rules.watch: Uniqueness is a separate proof.
rules.when: 'There is a unique…'.

rules.formula: \( \neg \forall x\,(P(x) \to Q(x)) \equiv \exists x\,(P(x) \wedge \neg Q(x)) \)
rules.name: Counterexample
rules.watch: The example must satisfy the hypothesis.
rules.when: Disproving a universal claim.

stuck: Write down the logical form of the goal (\( \forall, \exists, \to, \leftrightarrow, \vee \)) and let it choose the method.
Unfold every definition in both the hypothesis and the conclusion, then look for how to connect the equations.
If the hypothesis gives nothing to compute with, try the contrapositive; if the statement is negative ('no', 'not', 'irrational', 'infinitely many'), try contradiction.
Test small, zero, negative and equal values; a counterexample or the reason none exists often appears.
If an expression's parity or remainder matters, split into cases by parity or by remainder mod the relevant number.

kps.d: State the definitions of even, odd, divides, prime, rational, and unfold them correctly as givens or goals.
Set up a proof from the logical form of the statement: arbitrary elements for ∀, witnesses for ∃, assume hypothesis for →.
Prove P → Q by assuming P and deducing Q, with correct variable handling.
Recognize when contraposition helps, state the contrapositive correctly, and prove it.
Negate the statement correctly, derive a genuine contradiction, and distinguish the method from contraposition.
Reproduce and adapt the irrationality of √2 and Euclid's proof of infinitely many primes.
Split into exhaustive cases (parity, remainders, sign) and handle each; use WLOG only for genuinely symmetric cases.
Prove P ↔ Q by proving both directions, possibly by different methods.
Give constructive existence proofs and recognize non-constructive ones.
Prove existence and uniqueness as two separate parts.
Refute a universal claim with a verified counterexample satisfying the hypothesis.

practice.model: *Proof.* Let \( m, n \) be odd: \( m = 2k + 1 \), \( n = 2l + 1 \) for integers \( k, l \). Then \( mn = 4kl + 2k + 2l + 1 = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1 \). Since \( 2kl + k + l \) is an integer, \( mn \) is odd. \( \blacksquare \)
practice.prompt: Give a direct proof that the product of two odd integers is odd.
rubric: Assumes m = 2k + 1, n = 2l + 1 with distinct integers k, l
Computes mn = 4kl + 2k + 2l + 1
Writes mn = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1
Concludes mn is odd since 2kl + k + l is an integer
practice.why: Unfold both hypotheses with separate variables, multiply, and regroup into the form \( 2j + 1 \).

practice.model:
*Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, that \( x^{2} - 6x + 5 \) is even and \( x \) is not odd, so \( x \) is even: \( x = 2a \). Then \( x^{2} - 6x + 5 = 4a^{2} - 12a + 5 = 2(2a^{2} - 6a + 2) + 1 \), which is odd. So \( x^{2} - 6x + 5 \) is both even and odd, which is impossible. Hence \( x \) is odd. \(  lacksquare \)

The contrapositive proof is cleaner: the contradiction argument used the hypothesis only at the very end, to clash with a conclusion that was derived from \( 
eg Q \) alone. That is exactly a proof of \( 
eg Q 	o 
eg P \) in disguise.
practice.prompt: Prove that for every integer \( x \), if \( x^{2} - 6x + 5 \) is even, then \( x \) is odd, using a method different from the one in the section text: prove it by contradiction instead of by contrapositive. Then comment on which write-up is cleaner and why.
rubric: Assumes x² − 6x + 5 even and x even (negation of conclusion)
With x = 2a shows x² − 6x + 5 = 2(2a² − 6a + 2) + 1 is odd
Contradiction: the number is both even and odd
Comments that the contrapositive version is cleaner because the hypothesis was never used except to contradict
practice.why: If a contradiction proof reaches \( \neg P \) from \( \neg Q \) alone, rewrite it as a contrapositive proof.

practice.model: *Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, that integers \( a, b \) satisfy \( 18a + 6b = 1 \). Then \( 6(3a + b) = 1 \), so \( 3a + b = \frac{1}{6} \). But \( 3a + b \) is an integer and \( \frac{1}{6} \) is not. This contradiction shows no such integers exist. \( \blacksquare \)
practice.prompt: Prove that there are no integers \( a \) and \( b \) such that \( 18a + 6b = 1 \).
rubric: Assumes for contradiction integers a, b with 18a + 6b = 1
Factors 18a + 6b = 6(3a + b)
Deduces 6 | 1 or 1/6 = 3a + b is an integer
Contradiction since 1/6 is not an integer
practice.why: Every integer combination of 18 and 6 is a multiple of 6, and 1 is not.

practice.model: *Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, that \( \log_{2} 3 = \frac{a}{b} \) for integers \( a, b \) with \( b \neq 0 \). Since \( 3 > 1 \), \( \log_{2} 3 > 0 \), so we may take \( a, b > 0 \). Then \( 2^{a/b} = 3 \), and raising to the power \( b \), \( 2^{a} = 3^{b} \). The left side is even because \( a \ge 1 \); the right side is odd, being a product of odd numbers. An integer cannot be both, so this is a contradiction. Hence \( \log_{2} 3 \) is irrational. \( \blacksquare \)
practice.prompt: Prove that \( \log_{2} 3 \) is irrational.
rubric: Assumes log₂ 3 = a/b with integers, and notes log₂ 3 > 0 so a, b can be taken positive
Derives 2^{a/b} = 3, hence 2^a = 3^b
Observes 2^a is even (a ≥ 1) and 3^b is odd
Contradiction, so irrational
practice.why: Clearing the fraction turns an irrationality claim into a statement about integers where parity gives the contradiction.

practice.model: *Proof.* Let \( n = 2k + 1 \). Then \( n^{2} - 1 = 4k^{2} + 4k = 4k(k + 1) \). We claim \( k(k + 1) \) is even. If \( k \) is even, \( k = 2j \) and \( k(k + 1) = 2\,j(k + 1) \). If \( k \) is odd, \( k + 1 = 2j \) and \( k(k + 1) = 2\,kj \). Either way \( k(k + 1) = 2m \) for an integer \( m \), so \( n^{2} - 1 = 8m \), and \( 8 \mid (n^{2} - 1) \). \( \blacksquare \)
practice.prompt: Prove that for every odd integer \( n \), \( 8 \mid (n^{2} - 1) \).
rubric: Writes n = 2k + 1 and computes n² − 1 = 4k² + 4k = 4k(k + 1)
Notes k(k + 1) is even (product of consecutive integers), justified by cases on the parity of k
Writes k(k + 1) = 2m
Concludes n² − 1 = 8m
practice.why: A direct computation reduces the problem to a small lemma proved by cases.

practice.model:
*Proof.* (\( \Rightarrow \)) If \( n = 2k \), then \( 7n + 4 = 14k + 4 = 2(7k + 2) \), which is even.

(\( \Leftarrow \)) We prove the contrapositive: if \( n \) is odd, then \( 7n + 4 \) is odd. If \( n = 2k + 1 \), then \( 7n + 4 = 14k + 11 = 2(7k + 5) + 1 \), which is odd.

Both directions hold, so \( n \) is even iff \( 7n + 4 \) is even. \( \blacksquare \)
practice.prompt: Prove that for every integer \( n \), \( n \) is even if and only if \( 7n + 4 \) is even. Use a direct proof in one direction and a contrapositive proof in the other.
rubric: (⇒) direct: n = 2k gives 7n + 4 = 2(7k + 2)
(⇐) contrapositive: assume n odd, n = 2k + 1
Computes 7n + 4 = 14k + 11 = 2(7k + 5) + 1, odd
Both directions labeled and concluded
practice.why: Each direction of a biconditional is a separate conditional, and each may use its own method.

practice.prompt: The claim "\( n^{2} + n + 41 \) is prime for every integer \( n \ge 0 \)" is false. What is the smallest counterexample \( n \)?
practice.why: Checking \( n = 0, 1, \dots, 39 \) gives primes each time; at \( n = 40 \), \( 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41^{2} \). (A computer check confirms all 40 earlier values are prime.)

practice.model:
The write-up starts from the conclusion and derives a true statement. That establishes "if \( x^{2} + 1 \ge 2x \) then \( (x - 1)^{2} \ge 0 \)", and concluding the hypothesis from the truth of the conclusion is affirming the consequent. (From \( 1 = 2 \) one can derive the true \( 0 \cdot 1 = 0 \cdot 2 \).)

The claim is true, because each step is reversible. *Proof.* Let \( x \in \mathbb{R} \). Then \( (x - 1)^{2} \ge 0 \), so \( x^{2} - 2x + 1 \ge 0 \), so \( x^{2} + 1 \ge 2x \). \( \blacksquare \)
practice.prompt: A student proves "for all real \( x \), \( x^{2} + 1 \ge 2x \)" as follows: "\( x^{2} + 1 \ge 2x \). So \( x^{2} - 2x + 1 \ge 0 \). So \( (x - 1)^{2} \ge 0 \), which is true. Therefore \( x^{2} + 1 \ge 2x \)." Explain exactly what is logically wrong with the write-up, whether the claim is nevertheless true, and give a correct proof.
rubric: Identifies that the argument assumes the conclusion and derives a true statement (affirming the consequent)
Notes that deriving a truth from a claim does not prove the claim
Observes each step is reversible, so the claim is true
Gives the forward proof from (x − 1)² ≥ 0
practice.why: Scratch work may run backward; the proof must run forward from known facts.

options: If \( a \) and \( b \) are both odd, then \( ab \) is odd.
If \( a \) is odd or \( b \) is odd, then \( ab \) is odd.
If \( a \) is even or \( b \) is even, then \( ab \) is even.
If \( ab \) is odd, then \( a \) and \( b \) are both odd.
practice.prompt: You want to prove "for all integers \( a, b \), if \( ab \) is even then \( a \) is even or \( b \) is even". What is the contrapositive you would prove?
practice.why: The negation of "\( a \) even or \( b \) even" is, by De Morgan, "\( a \) odd and \( b \) odd". So the contrapositive is "if \( a \) and \( b \) are both odd, then \( ab \) is odd". The second option negates the "or" without switching to "and" (and is false: \( a = 1, b = 2 \)). The third is the converse. The fourth is the inverse.

practice.model:
A constructive proof names a specific object and verifies the property; a non-constructive proof shows that an object must exist without saying which.

In the proof about \( a^{b} \), we consider \( \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} \): if it is rational, take \( a = b = \sqrt{2} \); if irrational, take \( a = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} \), \( b = \sqrt{2} \), since then \( a^{b} = \sqrt{2}^{2} = 2 \). One case must hold, so a pair exists, but the proof does not tell us which pair. To make it constructive we would need to decide the case; the Gelfond–Schneider theorem shows \( \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} \) is irrational, so \( a = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} \), \( b = \sqrt{2} \) works. (Another constructive example: \( a = \sqrt{2} \), \( b = \log_{2} 9 \), since \( \sqrt{2}^{\log_{2} 9} = 2^{\frac{1}{2}\log_{2} 9} = 3 \) and \( \log_{2} 9 = 2\log_{2} 3 \) is irrational.)
practice.prompt: Explain the difference between a constructive and a non-constructive existence proof, and illustrate with the proof that there exist irrational \( a, b \) with \( a^{b} \) rational. Why is that proof non-constructive, and what would make it constructive?
rubric: Constructive: exhibits a specific object and verifies it
Non-constructive: proves existence without identifying the object
The √2^√2 proof splits into cases without deciding which holds, so it does not identify a and b
A constructive version requires knowing whether √2^√2 is irrational (it is, by Gelfond–Schneider), giving a = √2^√2, b = √2
practice.why: Non-constructive proofs often proceed by cases or by contradiction and leave the witness undetermined.

practice.model: *Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, that some integer \( n \) is both even and odd: \( n = 2a \) and \( n = 2b + 1 \) for integers \( a, b \). Then \( 2a = 2b + 1 \), so \( 2(a - b) = 1 \) and \( a - b = \frac{1}{2} \). But \( a - b \) is an integer and \( \frac{1}{2} \) is not. Hence no integer is both even and odd. \( \blacksquare \)
practice.prompt: Prove that no integer is both even and odd.
rubric: Assumes for contradiction n = 2a and n = 2b + 1
Derives 2(a − b) = 1
Notes a − b = 1/2 is not an integer (or 1 is not even)
Concludes contradiction
practice.why: This fact is what makes "\( n \) is both even and odd" a genuine contradiction in parity arguments.

mth-6-1.scope: Direct, contrapositive, contradiction and case proofs, biconditional, existence, uniqueness and counterexample arguments on elementary number-theoretic and real-number statements; induction and set proofs are left to later topics.

sections.md:
Before any strategy can be applied, you must know exactly what you are allowed to assume and exactly what you must reach. This section sets up that framework: definitions as the raw material of proofs, and the logical form of the goal as the guide to structure.

**Definitions are the tools.** A proof about even numbers cannot use a vague sense of "evenness"; it uses the definition. The definitions used throughout this course are:

> An integer \( n \) is **even** if \( n = 2k \) for some integer \( k \); it is **odd** if \( n = 2k + 1 \) for some integer \( k \).
>
> For integers \( a \) and \( b \), \( a \) **divides** \( b \), written \( a \mid b \), if \( b = ac \) for some integer \( c \).
>
> A natural number \( p > 1 \) is **prime** if its only positive divisors are \( 1 \) and \( p \); a natural number \( n > 1 \) that is not prime is **composite**.
>
> A real number \( x \) is **rational** if \( x = \frac{a}{b} \) for some integers \( a, b \) with \( b \neq 0 \); otherwise it is **irrational**.

We also use two basic facts about integers: every integer is either even or odd, and no integer is both. (Both follow from the division algorithm; the second is proved in the practice problems.) Two integers have the **same parity** if both are even or both are odd.

Notice that every definition is an existential statement ("for some integer \( k \)"). This dictates how definitions enter a proof. When a definition is **given** (assumed), you may name the integer it provides: "since \( n \) is even, \( n = 2k \) for some integer \( k \)". When a definition is the **goal**, you must produce the integer: to show \( m \) is even, exhibit an integer \( j \) and verify \( m = 2j \).

**Givens and goal.** At every stage of a proof there is a list of statements you may use (the givens) and one statement you must prove (the goal). The logical form of the goal tells you how to proceed (this is the approach of Velleman's *How to Prove It*):

- Goal \( P \to Q \): add \( P \) to the givens; the new goal is \( Q \).
- Goal \( \forall x\, P(x) \): introduce an **arbitrary** element: "let \( x \) be an arbitrary element of the domain". Assume nothing about \( x \) beyond its membership in the domain, and prove \( P(x) \). Since \( x \) was arbitrary, the argument works for every element.
- Goal \( \exists x\, P(x) \): find a specific **witness** \( a \) and prove \( P(a) \).
- Goal \( P \wedge Q \): prove \( P \) and prove \( Q \).

**Worked example.** Prove: for all integers \( m \) and \( n \), if \( m \) is even then \( mn \) is even.

1. Form: \( \forall m\, \forall n\, (m \text{ even} \to mn \text{ even}) \). So: let \( m \) and \( n \) be arbitrary integers, and assume \( m \) is even. Goal: \( mn \) is even.
2. Unfold the given: \( m = 2k \) for some integer \( k \).
3. Unfold the goal: we need an integer \( j \) with \( mn = 2j \).
4. Compute: \( mn = (2k)n = 2(kn) \). Take \( j = kn \), an integer because products of integers are integers.
5. Hence \( mn \) is even. Since \( m, n \) were arbitrary, the statement holds for all integers.

The common mistakes at this stage are **proof by example** (checking \( m = 4, n = 3 \) proves only that instance) and treating a goal as a given (writing "\( mn = 2j \)" at the start, before \( j \) has been found). Write the proof so that each line is justified by the givens and lines above it.

questions.model:
(a) Let \( a, b, c \) be arbitrary integers. Givens: \( a \mid b \) and \( a \mid c \). Goal: \( a \mid (b + c) \).

(b) The hypotheses are given, so they supply integers: \( b = ak \) and \( c = al \) for some integers \( k, l \) (different letters, since there is no reason they are equal). The conclusion is a goal, so we must produce an integer \( m \) with \( b + c = am \).

(c) *Proof.* Let \( a, b, c \) be integers with \( a \mid b \) and \( a \mid c \). Then \( b = ak \) and \( c = al \) for some integers \( k, l \). So \( b + c = ak + al = a(k + l) \). Since \( k + l \) is an integer, \( a \mid (b + c) \). \( \blacksquare \)
questions.prompt: For the statement "for all integers \( a, b, c \), if \( a \mid b \) and \( a \mid c \), then \( a \mid (b + c) \)": (a) list the givens and the goal after the proof has been set up; (b) say which definitions must be unfolded and whether each is used as a given (name the integer) or as a goal (produce the integer); (c) write the proof.
rubric: (a) a, b, c arbitrary integers; givens a | b and a | c; goal a | (b + c)
(b) a | b and a | c are unfolded as givens: b = ak, c = al for integers k, l; the goal a | (b + c) requires producing an integer m with b + c = am
(c) computes b + c = ak + al = a(k + l) and takes m = k + l, an integer
Uses distinct letters for the two integers given by the hypotheses
questions.why: Existential definitions are unpacked (named) when given and constructed when they are the goal.

questions.model: A universal statement "for all even \( m, n \), \( 4 \mid (m + n) \)" is not established by checking instances; a proof must treat \( m \) and \( n \) as arbitrary even integers. Here the claim is in fact false: \( 2 + 4 = 6 \), and \( 4 \nmid 6 \). One counterexample refutes a universal claim. (What is true is that \( m + n = 2k + 2l = 2(k + l) \) is even.)
questions.prompt: A student "proves" that the sum of any two even integers is divisible by 4 as follows: "\( 2 + 2 = 4 \), \( 4 + 4 = 8 \), \( 6 + 2 = 8 \), \( 8 + 4 = 12 \): all divisible by 4." Explain precisely what is wrong with this as a proof, and settle the claim.
rubric: Checking examples does not prove a universal statement; the variables must be arbitrary
The claim is false
Gives a counterexample, e.g. 2 + 4 = 6, which is not divisible by 4
Notes that a universal claim is refuted by a single counterexample
questions.why: Examples can suggest or refute a universal claim, but never prove it.

sections.title: Definitions, givens and goals

sections.md:
The simplest strategy for a conditional \( P \to Q \) is to assume \( P \) and reason forward to \( Q \). This section describes the method and the discipline needed to carry it out.

> **Direct proof** of \( P \to Q \): assume \( P \); using definitions, known results and valid inferences, deduce \( Q \).

The justification is the truth table of the conditional: \( P \to Q \) can fail only when \( P \) is true, so it suffices to show that \( Q \) is true in every situation where \( P \) is true. When the statement is universally quantified, as most theorems are, the variables are introduced as arbitrary first.

A useful working habit is to do **scratch work** in two directions before writing. Forward: unpack the hypothesis into equations. Backward: unpack the conclusion into what you need to produce. The proof is found where the two meet, then written cleanly from hypothesis to conclusion.

**Worked example 1.** Prove: if \( m \) and \( n \) are odd integers, then \( m + n \) is even.

*Scratch.* Forward: \( m = 2k + 1 \), \( n = 2l + 1 \). Backward: need \( m + n = 2j \) for an integer \( j \).

*Proof.* Suppose \( m \) and \( n \) are odd. Then \( m = 2k + 1 \) and \( n = 2l + 1 \) for some integers \( k, l \). Hence
\[ m + n = 2k + 2l + 2 = 2(k + l + 1). \]
Since \( k + l + 1 \) is an integer, \( m + n \) is even. \( \blacksquare \)

The letters \( k \) and \( l \) must be different. Writing \( m = 2k + 1 \) and \( n = 2k + 1 \) silently assumes \( m = n \), and the resulting "proof" covers only that case. This is one of the most common errors in first proofs.

**Worked example 2 (transitivity of divisibility).** Prove: for all integers \( a, b, c \), if \( a \mid b \) and \( b \mid c \), then \( a \mid c \).

*Proof.* Let \( a, b, c \) be integers with \( a \mid b \) and \( b \mid c \). Then \( b = ak \) and \( c = bl \) for some integers \( k, l \). Substituting the first equation into the second,
\[ c = (ak)l = a(kl). \]
Since \( kl \) is an integer, \( a \mid c \). \( \blacksquare \)

**Worked example 3 (inequality).** Prove: for all real numbers \( x \) and \( y \), \( x^{2} + y^{2} \ge 2xy \).

*Scratch.* Rearranging the goal gives \( x^{2} - 2xy + y^{2} \ge 0 \), that is, \( (x - y)^{2} \ge 0 \), which is true. But this scratch runs from the goal to a known fact, which is the wrong direction for a proof (it would be affirming the consequent). Each step, however, is reversible, so we write it forward.

*Proof.* Let \( x, y \in \mathbb{R} \). The square of a real number is nonnegative, so \( (x - y)^{2} \ge 0 \). Expanding, \( x^{2} - 2xy + y^{2} \ge 0 \). Adding \( 2xy \) to both sides gives \( x^{2} + y^{2} \ge 2xy \). \( \blacksquare \)

**Writing conventions.** State what you are assuming; write in complete sentences, with symbols embedded in them; justify every step that is not routine algebra; mark the end with \( \blacksquare \) or "Q.E.D.". A proof is written for a reader, not as a record of how you found it.

**The common mistakes**: reusing a letter for integers that need not be equal; starting from the conclusion and deriving something true (valid only if every step reverses, and the write-up must then run forward); and using the claim itself as a step.

\[ bx + cy = (ak)x + (al)y = a(kx + ly). \]
Since \( k, l, x, y \) are integers, so is \( kx + ly \). Therefore \( a \mid (bx + cy) \). \( \blacksquare \)

The error is writing both \( m = 2k \) and \( n = 2k \): the definition of evenness gives *some* integer for each, and there is no reason for them to be the same. Using one letter assumes \( m = n \), so the argument proves only that \( 4 \mid m^{2} \) for even \( m \).

*Correct proof.* Let \( m, n \) be even. Then \( m = 2k \) and \( n = 2l \) for some integers \( k, l \). So \( mn = 4kl \). Since \( kl \) is an integer, \( 4 \mid mn \). \( \blacksquare \)
