sections.title: Direct proof

sections.md:
Some conditionals resist a direct attack: assuming the hypothesis gives you little to work with, while the negation of the conclusion would give a great deal. This section shows how to exploit the logical equivalence of a conditional with its contrapositive.

> **Proof by contrapositive** of \( P \to Q \): assume \( \neg Q \); deduce \( \neg P \).

Since \( P \to Q \equiv \neg Q \to \neg P \) (a truth-table fact from the logic topic), a direct proof of \( \neg Q \to \neg P \) is a proof of \( P \to Q \). No new logic is involved; what changes is what you get to assume.

**When to use it.** Look at the two sides. If the hypothesis \( P \) is complicated or does not unpack usefully, while \( \neg Q \) gives a concrete equation, contraposition is often easier. A typical signal: the conclusion is "\( n \) is even" or "\( n \) is odd" and the hypothesis is a statement about \( n^{2} \) or some expression in \( n \). Assuming "\( n^{2} \) is even" gives \( n^{2} = 2k \), and there is no clean way to extract \( n \) from that. Assuming "\( n \) is odd" gives \( n = 2k + 1 \), which can be squared.

**Worked example 1.** Prove: for every integer \( n \), if \( n^{2} \) is even, then \( n \) is even.

*Why not directly?* From \( n^{2} = 2k \) we would want \( n = \sqrt{2k} \), which leads nowhere: it is not even clear that it is an integer expression of the right form.

*Proof.* We prove the contrapositive: if \( n \) is not even, then \( n^{2} \) is not even; that is, if \( n \) is odd then \( n^{2} \) is odd. Suppose \( n \) is odd, so \( n = 2k + 1 \) for some integer \( k \). Then
\[ n^{2} = 4k^{2} + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^{2} + 2k) + 1, \]
and \( 2k^{2} + 2k \) is an integer, so \( n^{2} \) is odd. By contraposition, if \( n^{2} \) is even then \( n \) is even. \( \blacksquare \)

This lemma will be used in the next section to prove that \( \sqrt{2} \) is irrational.

**Worked example 2.** Prove: for every integer \( x \), if \( x^{2} - 6x + 5 \) is even, then \( x \) is odd.

*Proof.* We prove the contrapositive: if \( x \) is even, then \( x^{2} - 6x + 5 \) is odd. Suppose \( x = 2a \) for an integer \( a \). Then
\[ x^{2} - 6x + 5 = 4a^{2} - 12a + 5 = 2(2a^{2} - 6a + 2) + 1, \]
and \( 2a^{2} - 6a + 2 \) is an integer, so \( x^{2} - 6x + 5 \) is odd. \( \blacksquare \)

**Writing it up.** Always announce the method ("We prove the contrapositive…") and state the contrapositive explicitly, so the reader knows what is being assumed and what is the goal. Negate carefully: using the logic topic, "not even" becomes "odd" (for integers), "\( a \mid b \)" becomes "\( a \nmid b \)", and "\( x > 0 \)" becomes "\( x \le 0 \)". When the statement has several hypotheses or a compound conclusion, the negation follows De Morgan: the contrapositive of \( P \to (Q \wedge R) \) is \( (\neg Q \vee \neg R) \to \neg P \), which usually splits into cases.

**The common mistake** is to prove the converse \( Q \to P \) or the inverse \( \neg P \to \neg Q \) instead of the contrapositive. Both are logically different from the original. For worked example 1, the converse "if \( n \) is even then \( n^{2} \) is even" is true but proving it does not prove the lemma.

questions.model:
Contrapositive: "If \( n \) is even, then \( 5n + 3 \) is odd."

*Proof.* Suppose \( n \) is even, so \( n = 2k \) for some integer \( k \). Then \( 5n + 3 = 10k + 3 = 2(5k + 1) + 1 \), and \( 5k + 1 \) is an integer, so \( 5n + 3 \) is odd. This proves the contrapositive, and hence the original statement. \( \blacksquare \)

The second option is the inverse; the third is the converse (true, but not the statement). The fourth is a valid proof by contradiction, but it is a different method, not the contrapositive.

sections.title: Proof by contrapositive

sections.md:
Some statements have no convenient hypothesis to work from at all, "\( \sqrt{2} \) is irrational" for instance, or are negative claims ("there is no largest prime"). This section develops a strategy that manufactures a hypothesis: assume the statement is false and show that this is impossible.

> **Proof by contradiction** of a statement \( P \): assume \( \neg P \), and deduce a **contradiction**, a statement of the form \( C \wedge \neg C \). Conclude \( P \).

The logic: \( \neg P \to (C \wedge \neg C) \) is equivalent to \( \neg \neg P \vee (C \wedge \neg C) \), which is equivalent to \( P \), because \( C \wedge \neg C \) is always false. So if \( \neg P \) leads to a contradiction, \( \neg P \) is false. For a conditional \( P \to Q \), since \( \neg (P \to Q) \equiv P \wedge \neg Q \), the method becomes: assume \( P \) and \( \neg Q \), and derive a contradiction.

The contradiction need not be announced in advance; it is anything that clashes with a given, a known fact, or another derived statement. That freedom is the strength of the method (you assume more) and its danger (you may not know what you are aiming for).

**Worked example 1.** Prove that \( \sqrt{2} \) is irrational.

*Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, that \( \sqrt{2} \) is rational. Then \( \sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b} \) for integers \( a, b \) with \( b \neq 0 \), and we may assume the fraction is in lowest terms: \( a \) and \( b \) are not both even (otherwise cancel a factor of 2, repeatedly if necessary). Squaring, \( 2 = \frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}} \), so \( a^{2} = 2b^{2} \). Thus \( a^{2} \) is even, and by the lemma of the previous section, \( a \) is even: \( a = 2c \) for an integer \( c \). Substituting, \( 4c^{2} = 2b^{2} \), so \( b^{2} = 2c^{2} \) is even, and again by the lemma \( b \) is even. Now \( a \) and \( b \) are both even, contradicting the choice of lowest terms. Hence \( \sqrt{2} \) is irrational. \( \blacksquare \)

**Worked example 2 (Euclid).** Prove that there are infinitely many primes. We use the fact that every natural number greater than 1 has a prime divisor (this will be proved by strong induction in the next topic).

*Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, \( p_{1}, p_{2}, \dots, p_{k} \). Let
\[ N = p_{1} p_{2} \cdots p_{k} + 1. \]
Since \( N > 1 \), \( N \) has a prime divisor \( q \), and \( q \) must be one of the \( p_{i} \). Then \( q \mid p_{1} \cdots p_{k} \) and \( q \mid N \), so \( q \) divides \( N - p_{1} \cdots p_{k} = 1 \). But no prime divides 1, since primes exceed 1. This contradiction shows there are infinitely many primes. \( \blacksquare \)

Note what the proof does *not* claim: \( N \) need not itself be prime. For the first six primes, \( 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509 \).

**Contradiction versus contrapositive.** For \( P \to Q \), contraposition assumes \( \neg Q \) and has a fixed target, \( \neg P \). Contradiction assumes both \( P \) and \( \neg Q \) and accepts any contradiction. If your contradiction proof ends by deriving \( \neg P \) from \( \neg Q \) alone, it was really a contrapositive proof and is clearer written that way.

**The common mistakes**: negating the statement incorrectly at the start (use the negation rules from the logic topic); stopping at a statement that merely looks odd rather than an actual contradiction; and, in example 1, forgetting the lowest-terms assumption, without which "both even" is not a contradiction.

The statement is "there is no positive rational \( r \) such that \( r \le s \) for every positive rational \( s \)". Its negation: there exists a positive rational \( r \) with \( r \le s \) for every positive rational \( s \).

*Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, that such an \( r \) exists; write \( r = \frac{a}{b} \) with integers \( a, b \), \( b \neq 0 \). Then \( \frac{r}{2} = \frac{a}{2b} \) is rational, and it is positive since \( r > 0 \). By the choice of \( r \), \( r \le \frac{r}{2} \). But \( r > 0 \) gives \( \frac{r}{2} < r \). sections.title: Proof by contradiction

sections.md:
Two situations call for splitting a proof into parts: when the hypothesis naturally divides into possibilities that must be handled differently, and when the statement is a biconditional, which is two conditionals at once. This section treats both.

> **Proof by cases.** To prove \( Q \), find statements \( P_{1}, \dots, P_{k} \) such that \( P_{1} \vee \cdots \vee P_{k} \) is known to be true (the cases are **exhaustive**), and prove \( P_{i} \to Q \) for each \( i \).

This is the valid argument form "\( P \vee R \), \( P \to Q \), \( R \to Q \), therefore \( Q \)" from the logic topic, extended to \( k \) cases. The cases need not be mutually exclusive, but they must cover every possibility. Common splits: \( n \) even or odd; the remainder of \( n \) on division by 3 is 0, 1 or 2; \( x \ge 0 \) or \( x < 0 \).

**Worked example 1.** Prove: for every integer \( n \), \( n^{2} + 3n + 5 \) is odd.

*Proof.* Let \( n \) be an integer. Every integer is even or odd.

*Case 1: \( n \) even*, \( n = 2k \). Then \( n^{2} + 3n + 5 = 4k^{2} + 6k + 5 = 2(2k^{2} + 3k + 2) + 1 \), which is odd.

*Case 2: \( n \) odd*, \( n = 2k + 1 \). Then \( n^{2} + 3n + 5 = 4k^{2} + 4k + 1 + 6k + 3 + 5 = 4k^{2} + 10k + 9 = 2(2k^{2} + 5k + 4) + 1 \), which is odd.

The cases are exhaustive, so \( n^{2} + 3n + 5 \) is odd for every integer \( n \). \( \blacksquare \)

**Without loss of generality.** When two cases are symmetric (the same argument works after renaming), one may write "**without loss of generality** (WLOG), assume \( m \) is even" and treat one case, provided the symmetry is genuine. For example, to show that if \( mn \) is odd then both are odd, one may handle "\( m \) even" and note that "\( n \) even" is identical with the roles exchanged.

> **Biconditional proofs.** To prove \( P \leftrightarrow Q \), prove \( P \to Q \) and \( Q \to P \). Each direction may use a different method.

Label the directions clearly: "(\( \Rightarrow \))" for \( P \to Q \) and "(\( \Leftarrow \))" for \( Q \to P \). To prove that several statements \( P_{1}, \dots, P_{k} \) are all equivalent, it suffices to prove a cycle \( P_{1} \to P_{2} \to \cdots \to P_{k} \to P_{1} \).

**Worked example 2.** Prove: for every integer \( n \), \( n \) is even if and only if \( n^{2} \) is even.

*Proof.* (\( \Rightarrow \)) Suppose \( n \) is even, \( n = 2k \). Then \( n^{2} = 4k^{2} = 2(2k^{2}) \) is even. (\( \Leftarrow \)) This is the lemma proved by contrapositive in the section on contraposition: if \( n \) is odd, \( n^{2} \) is odd. Both directions hold. \( \blacksquare \)

The example shows a direct proof in one direction and a contrapositive proof in the other; this mixing is normal.

**The common mistakes**: omitting a case (for instance, forgetting negative numbers or zero when splitting by sign), using cases that do not cover all possibilities, claiming WLOG when the cases are not symmetric, and proving only one direction of a biconditional (usually the easier one).

questions.model:
*Proof.* Let \( n \) be an integer. By the division algorithm, \( n = 3k \), \( n = 3k + 1 \) or \( n = 3k + 2 \) for some integer \( k \); these cases are exhaustive. Note \( n^{3} - n = (n - 1)n(n + 1) \).

*Case \( n = 3k \):* \( n^{3} - n = 3k\,(3k - 1)(3k + 1) \), a multiple of 3.

*Case \( n = 3k + 1 \):* \( n - 1 = 3k \), so \( n^{3} - n = 3k\,(3k + 1)(3k + 2) \), a multiple of 3.

*Case \( n = 3k + 2 \):* \( n + 1 = 3k + 3 = 3(k + 1) \), so \( n^{3} - n = (3k + 1)(3k + 2) \cdot 3(k + 1) \), a multiple of 3.

In every case \( 3 \mid (n^{3} - n) \). \( \blacksquare \)

sections.title: Proof by cases and biconditional proofs

sections.md:
Not every theorem is a conditional. Many assert that something exists, that exactly one such thing exists, or (when you are refuting a claim) that a universal statement fails. This section covers the strategies matched to those logical forms.

**Existence.** To prove \( \exists x\, P(x) \), the most convincing method is a **constructive proof**: exhibit a specific \( a \) and verify \( P(a) \). For example, "there is an integer that can be written as a sum of two positive cubes in two different ways" is proved by \( 1729 = 1^{3} + 12^{3} = 9^{3} + 10^{3} \). A **non-constructive proof** establishes existence without identifying the object, often by contradiction or by cases.

**Worked example 1 (non-constructive).** Prove: there exist irrational numbers \( a, b \) such that \( a^{b} \) is rational.

*Proof.* Consider \( \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} \). It is either rational or irrational.

*Case 1:* it is rational. Take \( a = b = \sqrt{2} \), both irrational.

*Case 2:* it is irrational. Take \( a = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} \) and \( b = \sqrt{2} \). Then \( a^{b} = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}^{2} = 2 \), which is rational.

In either case suitable \( a, b \) exist. \( \blacksquare \)

The proof does not tell us which case holds. (It is known, by the Gelfond–Schneider theorem, that \( \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} \) is irrational, but the proof above needs no such fact.)

**Uniqueness.** "There is a unique \( x \) such that \( P(x) \)", written \( \exists! x\, P(x) \), means \( \exists x\, P(x) \) and at most one \( x \) satisfies \( P \). A proof has two parts:

1. *Existence:* find \( a \) with \( P(a) \).
2. *Uniqueness:* suppose \( P(y) \) and \( P(z) \) both hold, and prove \( y = z \). (Equivalently, suppose \( P(y) \) and show \( y = a \).)

**Worked example 2.** Prove: for every integer \( n \), there is a unique integer \( q \) and a unique \( r \in \{0, 1\} \) with \( n = 2q + r \).

*Existence.* If \( n \) is even, \( n = 2q + 0 \); if odd, \( n = 2q + 1 \). Every integer is even or odd.

*Uniqueness.* Suppose \( n = 2q + r = 2q' + r' \) with \( r, r' \in \{0, 1\} \). Then \( 2(q - q') = r' - r \). The right side is \( -1 \), \( 0 \) or \( 1 \), and the left side is even, so \( r' - r = 0 \). Then \( r = r' \) and \( 2(q - q') = 0 \) gives \( q = q' \). \( \blacksquare \)

This uniqueness also shows no integer is both even and odd.

**Disproof by counterexample.** To show that a universal statement \( \forall x\, P(x) \) is false, prove its negation \( \exists x\, \neg P(x) \): exhibit one \( a \) with \( P(a) \) false. Nothing more is needed, and checking a thousand agreeing cases is no defence against one counterexample.

**Worked example 3.** Disprove: for every natural number \( n \), \( n^{2} + n + 41 \) is prime.

At \( n = 40 \): \( 40^{2} + 40 + 41 = 1600 + 81 = 1681 = 41^{2} \), which is composite. So the statement is false. (It holds for \( n = 0, 1, \dots, 39 \), which is exactly why examples are not proofs.) A counterexample can also be found by reasoning rather than search: at \( n = 41 \), every term is a multiple of 41, so \( 41 \mid (41^{2} + 41 + 41) \).

**Prove or disprove.** When a problem says "prove or disprove", test small and extreme cases first (zero, one, negatives, equal values). If a counterexample appears, it settles the matter; if none appears, the pattern of why none appears often becomes the proof.

**The common mistakes**: giving a "counterexample" that does not satisfy the hypothesis; proving only existence when uniqueness was also claimed; and, in a uniqueness proof, assuming \( y \neq z \) and then deriving \( y = z \) without noticing that this is a contradiction proof which could be written directly.

questions.model:
*Existence.* \( n = 3 \) is a positive integer and \( 3^{2} - 2 \cdot 3 - 3 = 9 - 6 - 3 = 0 \).

*Uniqueness.* Suppose \( m \) is a positive integer with \( m^{2} - 2m - 3 = 0 \). Factoring, \( (m - 3)(m + 1) = 0 \), so \( m = 3 \) or \( m = -1 \). Since \( m > 0 \), \( m \ne -1 \); hence \( m = 3 \). So every positive solution equals the one found. \( \blacksquare \)
questions.prompt: Prove that there is a unique positive integer \( n \) such that \( n^{2} - 2n - 3 = 0 \). Label the existence and uniqueness parts.
rubric: Existence: n = 3 is a positive integer and 9 − 6 − 3 = 0
Uniqueness: suppose m is a positive integer with m² − 2m − 3 = 0
Factors (m − 3)(m + 1) = 0, so m = 3 or m = −1
Rules out m = −1 as not positive, concluding m = 3
questions.why: Uniqueness is shown by taking an arbitrary solution and proving it equals the known one; here the positivity hypothesis eliminates the root \( -1 \).

questions.model: The statement is false. Take \( p = 11 \), which is prime. Then \( 2^{11} - 1 = 2048 - 1 = 2047 \), and \( 23 \cdot 89 = 2047 \) (since \( 23 \cdot 89 = 23 \cdot 90 - 23 = 2070 - 23 = 2047 \)). So \( 2^{11} - 1 \) is composite. (For \( p = 2, 3, 5, 7 \) the numbers \( 3, 7, 31, 127 \) are prime, so \( p = 11 \) is the smallest counterexample.)
questions.prompt: Prove or disprove: for every prime \( p \), the number \( 2^{p} - 1 \) is prime. Your answer must include a complete verification.
rubric: Declares the statement false
Gives a specific counterexample p = 11 (smallest)
Verifies 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047 = 23 · 89 by multiplication
Notes that 11 is prime, so the counterexample satisfies the hypothesis
questions.why: A counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis (\( p \) prime) and violate the conclusion.

terms.d: A finite sequence of statements, each a hypothesis, definition, previously established result, or a valid inference from earlier lines, ending in the statement to be proved.
\( n \) is even if \( n = 2k \) for some integer \( k \); odd if \( n = 2k + 1 \) for some integer \( k \).
\( a \mid b \) means \( b = ac \) for some integer \( c \).
A natural number \( p > 1 \) whose only positive divisors are 1 and \( p \).
A natural number greater than 1 that is not prime.
\( x \) is rational if \( x = a/b \) for integers \( a, b \) with \( b \neq 0 \); irrational otherwise.
The property of an integer being even or odd.
An element introduced with no assumptions beyond membership in the domain, so that what is proved about it holds for all elements; the method for proving \( \forall x\, P(x) \).
Proof of \( P \to Q \) by assuming \( P \) and deducing \( Q \).
Proof of \( P \to Q \) by assuming \( \neg Q \) and deducing \( \neg P \).
Proof of \( P \) by assuming \( \neg P \) and deducing a statement of the form \( C \wedge \neg C \).
Proof of \( Q \) from exhaustive cases \( P_{1} \vee \cdots \vee P_{k} \) by proving each \( P_{i} \to Q \).
A declaration that only one of several symmetric cases will be treated because the others follow by relabeling.
An existence proof that exhibits a specific object with the required property.
An existence proof that shows an object must exist without identifying it.
\( \exists! x\, P(x) \): some \( x \) satisfies \( P \), and any two elements satisfying \( P \) are equal.
A specific element satisfying the hypothesis of a universal claim but not its conclusion, disproving the claim.
A proved statement used mainly as a step toward a larger theorem.
At each stage of a proof, the statements you may use (givens) and the statement you must prove (goal); the logical form of the goal dictates the next step.
A specific object \( a \) exhibited to prove \( \exists x\, P(x) \) by verifying \( P(a) \).
Unrecorded exploration, forward from the hypotheses and backward from the goal, used to find a proof before writing it forward.
Cases \( P_{1}, \dots, P_{k} \) whose disjunction \( P_{1} \vee \cdots \vee P_{k} \) is known to be true, so that every possibility is covered.

mth-6-1.title: Proof techniques

cards.back: If \( P(a) \) holds and \( P(k) \to P(k+1) \) for every integer \( k \ge a \), then \( P(n) \) holds for every integer \( n \ge a \).
cards.front: State the principle of mathematical induction (starting at \( a \)).

cards.back: The assumption \( P(k) \), for an arbitrary integer \( k \ge a \), made inside the inductive step in order to deduce \( P(k+1) \).
cards.front: Define: inductive hypothesis

cards.back: \( k \) is one arbitrary integer and \( P(k) \) is the hypothesis of a conditional; the theorem \( \forall n\,P(n) \) is never assumed.
cards.front: Why is assuming \( P(k) \) in the inductive step not circular?
Give a false statement whose inductive step is valid.

cards.back: Separate the last term: \( \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} a_{i} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_{i} + a_{k+1} \), then apply the hypothesis.
cards.front: Standard first move in the inductive step for a sum formula

Least \( n_{0} \) such that \( 2^{n} > n^{2} \) for every \( n \ge n_{0} \)

cards.back: The stronger statement is also a stronger inductive hypothesis, which may supply exactly what the step needs.
cards.front: Why can a stronger statement be easier to prove by induction?

cards.back: If \( P(a) \) holds and, for every \( k \ge a \), \( P(a) \wedge \cdots \wedge P(k) \) implies \( P(k+1) \), then \( P(n) \) holds for all \( n \ge a \).
